The paper presents a deep learning approach for plasma tomography using the bolometer system at the Joint European Torus (JET) fusion device.
The authors used an up-convolutional neural network architecture, which is the inverse of a typical convolutional neural network (CNN).
The network was trained and tested on 4 separate datasets, each corresponding to a different JET campaign, with a total of around 18,000 sample reconstructions.
The authors used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to preprocess the input data from the 52 bolometer channels, determining that 50 components were sufficient to explain 100% of the variance.
The network was trained using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with a learning rate of 0.001, a batch size of 10, and Glorot-uniform weight initialization.
The training process for each dataset took around 17 hours to complete, with the network training for approximately 2000 epochs.
The authors evaluated the quality of the reconstructions using structural similarity (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and normalized root mean square error (NRMSE).
The average SSIM was around 0.99, indicating a high level of structural similarity between the original and reconstructed images.
The average PSNR was in the range of 30-50 dB, which is typical for high-quality image reconstruction.
The average NRMSE was between 2-4%, meaning the reconstruction error for each pixel was around 2-4% on average.

The authors suggest that this deep learning approach could be applied to other tomography diagnostics, such as soft X-ray cameras and neutron cameras, and could enable real-time tomographic reconstructions for plasma control.
The paper does not discuss potential limitations or future work, but notes that the approach could be used in other fusion devices besides JET.
The bolometer system at JET, known as KB5, comprises one horizontal camera (KB5H) and one vertical camera (KB5V) with a total of 24 bolometers each.
The KB5 system is able to collect readings at a sampling rate of 5 kHz, with each reading including the 24 channels of KB5H, the 24 channels of KB5V, and up to 8 additional reserve channels.
Previous tomographic reconstructions at JET were obtained through a series expansion of the plasma profile with a set of basis functions, with only a few reconstructions available per pulse.
